sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** DNS (Domain Name System) is a hierarchical, decentralized naming system that translates human-readable domain names like `api.example.com` into the IP addresses (IPv4 A records, IPv6 AAAA records) that network stacks actually use to open TCP connections, organized as a tree of authoritative servers starting at the root zone, delegating to TLDs (`.com`, `.org`), which delegate to per-domain authoritative servers.
DNS is the phonebook of the internet, but it is more accurately a distributed, eventually-consistent database with a strict delegation hierarchy. Every recursive resolution starts at the root nameservers (the 13 logical root addresses, anycast across hundreds of physical instances worldwide), which delegate to the appropriate TLD nameservers (`.com` operated by Verisign, `.org` by PIR, country-code TLDs by national registries), which in turn delegate to the domain's authoritative nameservers (typically operated by the registrar, a managed DNS provider like Route 53 or Cloudflare, or self-hosted). At each level, the response includes not just the answer but a TTL (time-to-live) telling resolvers how long to cache it. A typical full resolution is 4 queries: stub resolver → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative, though in practice the recursive resolver caches aggressively so most lookups hit cache after the first. The whole system is UDP-based on port 53 (with TCP fallback for responses over 512 bytes and for DNSSEC's large signatures), which makes DNS vulnerable to spoofing — the original protocol had no authentication, so an attacker on the path could inject fake responses and redirect users to malicious IPs.

DNS records are the data model. A records map a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA records (pronounced "quad-A") map to IPv6. CNAME aliases one name to another ("www.example.com CNAME example.com"), useful for pointing a subdomain at a CDN or SaaS endpoint without managing the underlying IPs. MX records specify mail exchange servers and their priority (lower number = higher priority). TXT records carry arbitrary text — used for SPF (sender policy framework), DKIM, domain ownership verification for ACME certificate issuance, and various service integrations. NS records declare which nameservers are authoritative for a zone. SOA records declare zone metadata (primary nameserver, admin email, serial, refresh/retry/expire timers). SRV records generalize service discovery (used by Active Directory, SIP, XMPP). PTR records do reverse lookups (IP → name). CAA records declare which CAs are allowed to issue certificates for a domain — a critical control after the DigiNotar compromise.

TTL is the single most important DNS parameter for system designers. A long TTL (1 hour to 1 day) means fewer queries to your authoritative servers, lower latency for users (cache hits), but slower propagation when you change an IP — a misconfigured record can take hours to fix. A short TTL (60 seconds) means you can reroute traffic in under a minute, but every resolver in the world hits your authoritative servers constantly, which raises query volume and cost. The convention for production traffic failover is 60–300 second TTLs so you can fail over to a backup region in minutes. For static content that never changes, 1-day TTLs are fine. Cloudflare famously uses a 5-minute default TTL on its free tier, which gives users a reasonable balance of caching and agility.

Real systems depend on DNS for much more than name resolution. AWS Route 53 (named after TCP port 53) provides latency-based routing, geolocation routing, weighted round-robin, and health-checked failover — Netflix uses these to route users to the closest regional fleet (US-East, EU-West, AP-Southeast) and to fail over to backup regions during outages. Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 and Google's 8.8.8.8 are public recursive resolvers optimized for speed — they run their own stacks instead of using the ISP's resolver, which is often slow and sometimes hijacked (some ISPs redirect NXDOMAIN responses to ad pages). GitHub's 2018 outage was caused by a DNS configuration mistake: a 24-hour TTL on a critical record meant that when they accidentally pointed it at the wrong IP, the bad result propagated globally and took hours to recover, even after the fix was pushed — because intermediate resolvers held the bad record until TTL expired.

DNSSEC is the cryptographic authentication layer that fixes DNS's spoofing vulnerability. It adds RRSIG (signature) records to each response, signed by the zone's private key, with the public key published as a DNSKEY record. The chain of trust starts at the root zone's KSK (key-signing key), which is published in the root trust anchor, and extends down through each zone's DS (delegation signer) record at the parent. A validating resolver (like 8.8.8.8 or systemd-resolved) walks the chain from the root, verifying each signature. DNSSEC does not encrypt DNS — that's what DNS-over-TLS (DoT, RFC 7858), DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484), and DNS-over-QUIC (DoQ) are for. Adoption of DNSSEC has been slow (~5–10% of domains signed) because key management is operationally fragile: forgetting to renew the ZSK (zone-signing key) before expiry breaks the zone for all validating resolvers, and there is no soft-fail path.

Split-horizon DNS is a powerful operational pattern: the same domain name resolves to different IPs depending on who is asking. Inside the corporate network, `wiki.acme.com` resolves to the internal IP; outside, it resolves to the public IP through a VPN gateway. Inside a Kubernetes cluster, the cluster DNS (CoreDNS) resolves `billing.svc.cluster.local` to the ClusterIP of the billing Service, while external traffic to `billing.acme.com` goes through an Ingress with TLS termination. This lets the same service name work both internally and externally without exposing internal IPs. The trade-off is consistency: if a service's internal and external IPs drift, debugging connectivity issues becomes a "where are you asking from" problem.

DNS connects to almost every other system design topic. It is the first step of every HTTP/HTTPS request — a 50 ms DNS lookup adds 50 ms to your TTFB SLO, which is why browsers and SDKs cache aggressively and why HTTP/3's connection migration benefits from short DNS TTLs. It is the substrate of service discovery in Kubernetes (CoreDNS), Consul, and Istio. It is how CDNs route users to the nearest edge PoP — Akamai, Cloudflare, and Fastly all use DNS-based geographic routing. The TTL parameter is a direct trade-off between cacheability and agility, echoing the latency-vs-throughput trade-off from Phase 1. DNS failures cascade: if your authoritative servers are down, the entire domain disappears from the internet in TTL seconds — which is why you always run multiple authoritative nameservers in different providers (Route 53 + Cloudflare, for example) and monitor DNS as a Tier-1 dependency.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant U as User Browser participant S as Stub Resolver participant R as Recursive Resolver (8.8.8.8) participant Root as Root Nameserver participant TLD as .com TLD Nameserver participant Auth as example.com Authoritative U->>S: getaddrinfo("api.example.com") S->>R: query api.example.com A Note over R: Check cache (TTL not expired?)
If hit: return cached IP, done. R->>Root: query api.example.com A Root-->>R: referral to .com TLD servers (NS + glue) R->>TLD: query api.example.com A TLD-->>R: referral to example.com authoritative (NS + glue) R->>Auth: query api.example.com A Auth-->>R: A 203.0.113.42 (TTL 300s) R-->>S: A 203.0.113.42 (TTL 300s) S-->>U: 203.0.113.42 Note over U: Browser opens TCP/TLS to 203.0.113.42:443 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +---------------------+ | User browser | | api.example.com ? | +----------+----------+ | v +---------------------+ | Stub resolver | | (libc / getaddrinfo)| +----------+----------+ | v +---------------------+---------------------+ | Recursive resolver (8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1) | | - has cache? hit -> return immediately | | - miss -> walk the hierarchy | +-----+---------------+---------------+-----+ | | | v v v +-----------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ | Root | | Root | | Root | | (a-m) | | (n-z) | | (anycast) | +-----+-----+ +-----+-----+ +-----+-----+ | | | +-------+-------+-------+-------+ | v referral: .com TLD NS list +-----------------+ | .com TLD | (Verisign) | gtld-servers | +--------+--------+ | v referral: example.com authoritative NS list +-----------------+ | example.com | (Route 53) | authoritative | | ns-123.awsdns | +--------+--------+ | v ANSWER: A 203.0.113.42 (TTL 300) +-----------------+ | Resolver cache | | api.example.com| | -> 203.0.113.42| | expires: T+300s| +-----------------+ Hierarchy: root (.) -- 13 logical, ~1500 physical instances (anycast) | +-- .com TLD -- operated by Verisign | +-- example.com -- operated by Route 53 | +-- api.example.com -- A 203.0.113.42 | +-- www.example.com -- CNAME example.com | +-- .org TLD -- operated by PIR +-- .io TLD -- operated by NIC.IO +-- .uk ccTLD -- operated by Nominet ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The browser calls `getaddrinfo("api.example.com")`, which delegates to the OS stub resolver. The stub resolver checks its local cache; on a miss, it forwards the query to the configured recursive resolver (e.g., `8.8.8.8` or the ISP's resolver). 2. The recursive resolver checks its cache. On a miss, it walks the hierarchy: asks the root nameserver for `api.example.com`, gets a referral to the `.com` TLD nameservers; asks the `.com` TLD, gets a referral to `example.com`'s authoritative nameservers; asks those, gets the final A record `203.0.113.42` with TTL 300. 3. The recursive resolver caches the answer for 300 seconds and returns it to the stub, which caches it locally and hands the IP to the browser. The browser can now open a TCP connection to `203.0.113.42:443`. Subsequent lookups within the TTL return from cache in microseconds.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Walk cache, then fall back to system resolver (which itself walks the root -> TLD -> authoritative hierarchy under the hood).
- Reference table of common DNS record types.
- Toy DNS resolver that walks the hierarchy using socket.getaddrinfo
- And demonstrates caching + TTL + record-type dispatch.
- 2. Cache miss -> ask the upstream system resolver.
- Socket.getaddrinfo internally walks root -> TLD -> authoritative.
- For non-A records, just record that we'd query authoritative.
- First lookup of a real domain -> upstream query + cache miss

**Defines:** `DNSRecord`, `RecursiveResolver`, `demonstrate_resolution_chain()`, `demonstrate_record_types()`

```python
# Toy DNS resolver that walks the hierarchy using socket.getaddrinfo
# and demonstrates caching + TTL + record-type dispatch.

import socket
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class DNSRecord:
    name: str
    rtype: str          # A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS
    value: str
    ttl: int
    expires_at: float   # epoch seconds

@dataclass
class RecursiveResolver:
    cache: dict = field(default_factory=dict)   # (name, rtype) -> DNSRecord
    query_log: list = field(default_factory=list)

    def _now(self) -> float:
        return time.time()

    def resolve(self, name: str, rtype: str = "A") -> Optional[DNSRecord]:
        """Walk cache, then fall back to system resolver (which itself walks
        the root -> TLD -> authoritative hierarchy under the hood)."""
        key = (name.lower(), rtype)
        # 1. Cache hit?
        rec = self.cache.get(key)
        if rec and rec.expires_at > self._now():
            self.query_log.append(("CACHE_HIT", name, rtype, rec.value))
            return rec
        if rec and rec.expires_at <= self._now():
            self.cache.pop(key, None)             # expired
        # 2. Cache miss -> ask the upstream system resolver.
        #    socket.getaddrinfo internally walks root -> TLD -> authoritative.
        self.query_log.append(("UPSTREAM_QUERY", name, rtype, "-"))
        try:
            if rtype in ("A", "AAAA"):
                family = socket.AF_INET if rtype == "A" else socket.AF_INET6
                results = socket.getaddrinfo(name, None, family=family,
                                             type=socket.SOCK_STREAM)
                if not results:
                    return None
                ip = results[0][4][0]
                ttl = 300                                   # default TTL for demo
                rec = DNSRecord(name, rtype, ip, ttl, self._now() + ttl)
                self.cache[key] = rec
                return rec
            # For non-A records, just record that we'd query authoritative.
            return DNSRecord(name, rtype, "<upstream-authoritative>", 300,
                             self._now() + 300)
        except socket.gaierror as e:
            self.query_log.append(("NXDOMAIN", name, rtype, str(e)))
            return None

    def show_cache(self) -> None:
        print("\n--- Resolver cache ---")
        for (name, rtype), rec in self.cache.items():
            remaining = max(0, int(rec.expires_at - self._now()))
            print(f"  {name:30s} {rtype:5s} -> {rec.value:20s}  ttl={remaining}s")

def demonstrate_resolution_chain():
    print("=== DNS Resolution Chain Demo ===\n")
    resolver = RecursiveResolver()

    # First lookup of a real domain -> upstream query + cache miss
    print("1. Resolving www.google.com (cold)...")
    rec = resolver.resolve("www.google.com", "A")
    print(f"   Answer: {rec.value if rec else 'NXDOMAIN'}")

    # Second lookup of the same -> cache hit
    print("\n2. Resolving www.google.com again (warm)...")
    rec = resolver.resolve("www.google.com", "A")
    print(f"   Answer: {rec.value if rec else 'NXDOMAIN'}")

    # Lookup a different domain -> another upstream query
    print("\n3. Resolving api.github.com (cold)...")
    rec = resolver.resolve("api.github.com", "A")
    print(f"   Answer: {rec.value if rec else 'NXDOMAIN'}")

    # AAAA record (IPv6)
    print("\n4. Resolving www.google.com AAAA (cold)...")
    rec = resolver.resolve("www.google.com", "AAAA")
    print(f"   Answer: {rec.value if rec else 'NXDOMAIN'}")

    # NXDOMAIN
    print("\n5. Resolving nonexistent-xyz-12345.example (NXDOMAIN)...")
    rec = resolver.resolve("nonexistent-xyz-12345.example", "A")
    print(f"   Answer: {rec.value if rec else 'NXDOMAIN'}")

    resolver.show_cache()

    print("\n--- Query log ---")
    for entry in resolver.query_log:
        print(f"  {entry[0]:18s} {entry[1]:35s} {entry[2]:5s} {entry[3]}")

def demonstrate_record_types():
    """Reference table of common DNS record types."""
    print("\n=== DNS Record Type Reference ===\n")
    records = [
        ("A",     "api.example.com",        "203.0.113.42",        "name -> IPv4"),
        ("AAAA",  "api.example.com",        "2001:db8::1",         "name -> IPv6"),
        ("CNAME", "www.example.com",        "example.com",         "alias to another name"),
        ("MX",    "example.com",            "10 mail1.example.com","mail exchange + priority"),
        ("TXT",   "_acme.example.com",      "validation-token-xyz","arbitrary text (SPF/DKIM/ACME)"),
        ("NS",    "example.com",            "ns-123.awsdns-03.com","authoritative nameserver"),
        ("SOA",   "example.com",            "ns-123 ... 2014030701 7200 900 1209600 86400",
                                                                      "zone metadata"),
        ("SRV",   "_sip._tcp.example.com",  "10 60 5060 sip.example.com", "service discovery"),
        ("PTR",   "42.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa", "api.example.com", "reverse lookup (IP -> name)"),
        ("CAA",   "example.com",            '0 issue "letsencrypt.org"',
                                                                      "which CA can issue certs"),
        ("DNSKEY","example.com",            "<base64 public key>", "DNSSEC signing key"),
        ("RRSIG", "example.com A",          "<base64 signature>",  "DNSSEC signature"),
    ]
    for rtype, name, value, purpose in records:
        print(f"  {rtype:7s} {name:35s} {value:40s}  # {purpose}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demonstrate_resolution_chain()
    demonstrate_record_types()
```

quiz.question: What happens when you type a URL into the browser, focusing on DNS?
options: Route 53 weighted routing is the standard answer.
Use Route 53 latency-based routing (LBR) with health-checked records.
The safe migration sequence has six steps.
The browser extracts the hostname (api.example.com) from the URL and calls getaddrinfo(), which goes to the OS stub resolver.
quiz.explanation: The browser extracts the hostname (api.example.com) from the URL and calls getaddrinfo(), which goes to the OS stub resolver. The stub checks its own cache (browsers also have their own DNS cache, separate from the OS). On a miss, the stub forwards the query to the configured recursive resolver — usually the one provided by DHCP, often 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, or the ISP's resolver.

quiz.explanation: DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions) adds cryptographic authentication to DNS responses, defeating cache poisoning and spoofing. It does not encrypt DNS — it just lets resolvers verify that a response genuinely came from the zone's authoritative server and was not tampered with on the wire. The mechanism: each zone has a key-signing key (KSK) and a zone-signing key (ZSK).
